name: The Release-Readiness Inspector
oneLiner: Replays every fixed bug's repro in a headless-capable Playwright browser, P1-first, and returns a pass-rate go/no-go verdict.
lead: Pulls the Closed/Resolved bugs under the features being released, runs a deterministic testability analysis to decide which can be automated, then drives a real Chromium session through each repro against your environment. Returns a release-readiness report — overall pass rate and a separate P1 pass rate — plus a screenshot per bug, most-critical first.
chore: Every release, a tester is supposed to re-open each fixed bug, read the repro, and manually click through to confirm it holds and nothing adjacent regressed. Across dozens of bugs under time pressure it gets rushed, and the urgent ones don't reliably get checked first.
instead: An automated re-check in a real browser, priority-ordered (P1 before P2/P3/P4), with a PASS/FAIL and screenshot per bug — plus an explicit SKIP list of what a browser genuinely cannot verify and why.
whyItMatters: A fix that quietly regressed erodes trust fast. This catches those regressions pre-ship, and the P1 pass rate is a hard go/no-go number a pipeline can gate on.

howItWorks.step: Collects Closed/Resolved bugs under the release features and sorts them P1-first.
howItWorks.explain: The two-level walk that assembles the re-check queue: features → their story IDs, then each story → its child work items. Because two release features can legitimately share a story, `Array.from(new Set(storyIds))` **dedups** before the child walk — otherwise a shared story's bugs would be tested (and counted) twice, distorting the pass rate. The inner guard keeps only items that are `WorkItemType === 'Bug'` **and** in `Closed`/`Resolved` — the point is to re-verify *fixed* bugs, so still-open ones are irrelevant. The final `sort` is what makes the gate meaningful under a `--limit`: `a.priority - b.priority` orders ascending (P1 = 1 first), and `.localeCompare` on `severity` only breaks ties **within** the same priority — so when only N bugs can run, the most critical ones are guaranteed to be the ones that do.

howItWorks.step: Per bug, a deterministic testability gate decides automatable vs skip — and records the skip reason.
howItWorks.explain: The honesty gate — it decides what a browser *can* truthfully verify, and everything it rejects gets a concrete reason rather than a silent pass. All four text sources are concatenated into one `combined` haystack so a disqualifying keyword is caught wherever it appears (title, repro, description, or tags). The three exits are ordered by cost: `findSkipReason` first rules out genuinely browser-impossible checks (microphone, visual-design judgment); then the `>= 20` content gate rejects repro text too thin to build reliable steps from — an `||` so **either** repro or description clearing the bar is enough; only then does `detectMode` attempt to map the bug to a known flow, skipping if it can't. Critically, a SKIP is **not** a FAIL — it returns `automatable: false` with `actions: []`, which keeps it out of the pass-rate denominator downstream. It's pure keyword matching, so no bug text ever leaves the machine.

howItWorks.step: Compiles the detected mode into a typed `ActionStep[]` — navigate, newChat, sendMessage, uploadFile, assertions.
howItWorks.explain: The compiler from an abstract `mode` to a concrete, replayable `ActionStep[]`. Every plan is bookended the same way — it **always** front-loads `navigate` + `newChat` so each bug starts from a known clean state (a stale session is a classic source of false failures), and **always** ends with a `screenshot` so there's visual evidence whether the run passes or throws. Inside a mode, sub-cases are chosen by keyword: `lower.includes('quiz')` appends the canonical **send → wait → assert** triple, where `assertResponseLength` with `minLength: 50` is the actual verification — it treats an empty or near-empty reply as a failure, catching a silently-broken feature that would otherwise look fine. The steps are plain data objects (`type` + optional `payload` + `description`), not calls — nothing touches the browser here; `executeAction` interprets them later.

howItWorks.step: Dispatches each `ActionStep` to a real Playwright command against the target environment.
howItWorks.explain: The interpreter that turns each data-only `ActionStep` into real Playwright calls. `sendMessage` resolves the input with `.first()` (defends against a selector that matches more than one node) and `waitFor({ state: 'visible', timeout: 10000 })` before typing — so a slow-rendering input surfaces as a clean 10s timeout, not a confusing `fill`-on-detached error. `waitForResponse` is the interesting one: rather than a fixed sleep, it **polls** the `thinkingText` indicator against a 90s `deadline`, and the moment `thinking` is false it waits one more `1500ms` settle beat and breaks — adapting to however long the app actually takes. The `.catch(() => false)` on `isVisible()` is deliberate: if the indicator element has already been removed from the DOM the check throws, and swallowing that to `false` correctly reads as 'not thinking / done' instead of crashing the whole bug run.

howItWorks.step: Runs a bug's full action sequence in a reset page and records PASS/FAIL with a screenshot and duration.
howItWorks.explain: The per-bug harness, and the whole thing is `try/catch`-shaped because **any** thrown action means the fix didn't hold — a failed `assertResponseLength`, a `waitFor` timeout, a missing element all funnel to the same FAIL. It calls `resetPageState(appUrl)` first so each bug is isolated from the last one's residue, then `await`s the actions **in order** (sequential, not parallel — order is the test). Reaching the end without throwing is the only PASS path. Two robustness details in the catch: `takeScreenshot(...).catch(() => undefined)` so that if even the failure screenshot fails, the result still returns rather than throwing out of the handler; and `(err.message || String(err)).slice(0, 250)` normalizes non-Error throws and **caps** the message at 250 chars to keep the report readable. `durationMs` is computed off the same `start` on both branches, so timing is recorded even for failures.

howItWorks.step: Rolls the per-bug results into a `ReleaseReport` — overall pass rate plus an isolated P1 pass rate.
howItWorks.explain: The verdict math, and its one crucial decision is what goes in the **denominator**. `tested` filters out `SKIP` before the rate is computed, so `passRate = passed / tested.length` measures only bugs the browser could actually verify — a mic-only bug that was honestly skipped can't inflate *or* deflate the number. The `tested.length > 0` guard returns `0` on an all-skipped run instead of dividing by zero. The P1 rate is computed the same way but over the `priority === 1 && status !== 'SKIP'` subset, kept **separate** because it's the hard gate a pipeline blocks on — you can ship with a stray P3 failure, but a failed P1 should stop the release regardless of how healthy the overall rate looks. Note `passed + failed` need not equal `tested.length` if any other non-skip status exists, so each count is derived independently rather than inferred.

examples.caption: P1 upload fix re-verified
examples.input: Closed bug `Document upload silently fails on the teaching screen`, priority 1.
examples.output: Playwright navigates, asserts the Upload button visible, `uploadFile`s a sample, waits for acknowledgement, records PASS with a screenshot and duration. P1, so it runs first.

examples.caption: Browser-impossible check, skipped honestly
examples.input: A fixed bug about voice-recording quality through the microphone.
examples.output: `findSkipReason` matches the mic keyword → SKIP, reason `Voice recording requires a microphone — cannot automate in a browser`. Excluded from the pass-rate denominator, flagged for manual check.

examples.caption: Regression caught
examples.input: A fixed bug where a menu should reappear after a new session.
examples.output: Agent starts a fresh session, the visibility assertion for the menu throws, records FAIL with the error (truncated) and a fail-state screenshot — drops the pass rate below the gate.

underHood.heading: Fetch closed bugs, P1-first
underHood.input: Feature IDs, or a saved tracker query URL.
underHood.output: Closed/Resolved bugs sorted by priority ascending — P1 runs before anything else.

underHood.heading: Deterministic testability gate
underHood.input: The bug's description, repro steps, and tags.
underHood.output: An automatable action plan, or a SKIP with a concrete reason (microphone, visual comparison, permission state, too-vague repro).

underHood.heading: Compile steps to ActionStep[]
underHood.output: A typed sequence: navigate, newChat, sendMessage, uploadFile, assertions, screenshot.

underHood.heading: Drive Chromium via Playwright
underHood.output: A real Playwright session — locate/fill/press/wait against live selectors, capturing the app's actual responses.

underHood.heading: Compute the go/no-go verdict
underHood.output: Overall pass rate plus an isolated P1 pass rate — the ship / no-ship gate metric.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
An Azure DevOps org/project and a **PAT** with work-item read scope.
A reachable running instance of the app under test (a dev/QA URL) and a way past its sign-in (SSO creds, or manual login on first run).
Playwright's Chromium binary installed — a real browser is driven per check, so this is mandatory.
No LLM key — testability decisions are deterministic keyword rules, kept fully local (no bug text leaves the machine).

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is TypeScript on Node. One-time per machine.
steps.firstRun: First time only, on a new machine.

steps.label: Install dependencies and the Chromium binary.
steps.cmd:
cd path/to/the-agents
npm install
npx playwright install chromium
steps.why: `npm install` pulls the ADO client and report writers; `playwright install` fetches the actual browser binary the agent drives. Skip it and the run fails immediately.
steps.firstRun: Dependencies plus a ~300MB browser binary — a few minutes.
steps.rerun: No-op once installed, unless the browser version changed.

steps.label: Export the ADO target and (optionally) sign-in (environment variables).
steps.cmd:
export ADO_ORGANIZATION=my-org
export ADO_PROJECT="My Project"
export ADO_PAT=your-access-token
export APP_SSO_PASSWORD=your-password   # optional — omit to log in by hand on first run
steps.why: Read at startup to resolve the board and, if the app's SSO page appears, get past it headlessly without a human at the keyboard.

steps.label: Dry-run the testability analysis — no browser yet.
steps.why: `--dry-run` fetches the closed bugs and runs testability analysis only — reports the automatable-vs-skip split before spending time driving Chromium.

steps.label: Run the real re-check against your environment.
steps.cmd:
npm run bug:release -- \
  --feature-ids "4001,4002" \
  --app-url https://qa.my-app.example.com \
  --limit 20

# or headless + a Word report in one go:
npm run bug:release:headless -- --app-url https://qa.my-app.example.com --word
steps.why: The actual re-check: drives Chromium, signs in, replays each bug's action sequence P1-first, capped at `--limit`.
steps.firstRun: May block on a manual SSO login if no password/session was configured.
steps.rerun: Faster once a saved session exists — later runs skip the login round-trip.

steps.label: Open the release-readiness report.
steps.why: The `.md` surfaces the overall and P1 pass rates; the screenshots folder holds one image per bug to eyeball anything FAIL or SKIP.

inputs.name: --feature-ids <ids>
inputs.desc: Comma-separated feature IDs to pull Closed/Resolved bugs from.

inputs.name: --query-url <url>
inputs.desc: A saved tracker query URL to source bugs from instead of walking features.

inputs.name: --env <dev|qa>
inputs.desc: Named environment to target, if --app-url isn't given.

inputs.name: --headless
inputs.desc: Run Chromium with no visible window (for CI).

inputs.name: --dry-run
inputs.desc: Testability analysis only — skip driving the browser.

inputs.name: --limit <n>
inputs.desc: Cap on automatable bugs actually run, P1 first (default 20).

inputs.name: environment variables
inputs.desc: Org/project target, the PAT, and (optionally) an SSO password.

outputs.name: BugRelease_<timestamp>.json
outputs.desc: Full structured report — PASS/FAIL/SKIP per bug, overall pass rate, P1 pass rate.

outputs.name: BugRelease_<timestamp>.md
outputs.desc: The same report rendered for a go/no-go read.

outputs.name: screenshots/
outputs.desc: One final-state screenshot per checked bug, PASS or FAIL.

runbook.rerun: No result caching — bug data and browser session are always fresh — but a saved sign-in session (once established) skips the manual-login wait on later runs. Re-run right before each release to catch anything that regressed since the last check.
runbook.integrate: Wire it as a release gate in CI — headless, against QA, after deploy and before promote-to-prod. Fail the pipeline when the pass rate (or specifically the P1 pass rate) drops below threshold, and archive the screenshots folder as release evidence.

video.caption: A 3-4 minute screen recording: fixed bugs re-checked live in a real Playwright browser before release.
script: Open a terminal next to a visible (non-headless) browser window so viewers can watch it click through the app.
Say: 'Before we ship, this agent re-checks every bug we already fixed — for real, in a browser. Watch.'
Run `node -v`, then `npx playwright install chromium`, noting it downloads the actual browser it will drive.
Show the `export ADO_ORGANIZATION / ADO_PROJECT / ADO_PAT` lines; say this is the only environment-specific config.
Run the `--dry-run` command; point out the testability split — 'these N it can check itself, these M need a human, and here's why.'
Run the real command without --headless; narrate as the browser opens, signs in, and replays one bug's steps live.
Pause on a PASS and point out the screenshot it just saved.
Pause on a FAIL (or describe one) — show the error message captured alongside its screenshot.
Open the produced `.md`; read out the overall pass rate and the P1-only pass rate.
Close: 'That's the go/no-go number for this release — checked by a browser, not a memory.'
